title: Adaptive tiling + prefetch profiling diary
body:
Purpose and high-level summary:

This working diary collects experiments and hypotheses for an adaptive tiling + prefetch policy aimed at improving attention kernel stability across mixed sequence-length workloads. Goal: reduce p95/p99 token latency spikes during microbursts while preserving TFLOPS efficiency and end-to-end throughput. We prototype three levers: tile_size (work granularity), prefetch_w (lookahead KV pages/prefetch slots), and fused-op fallbacks (enable/disable fused attention+softmax fusion). This doc is intentionally conversational — notes to self and team — and records commands, oddball artifacts, and concrete next experiments.

Context and why this matters:
- Production traces show intermittent 3–5x token latency spikes when a mix of short (16–64) and long (512–2048) requests run concurrently on the same GPU slab.
- Existing policy selects FlashAttention when sequence length > 128 and falls back to paged-flash for >1024; fused-paths are autopicked when batch shapes align. We suspect tiling boundaries and prefetch windowing cause bank conflicts and late kernel fallback that manifest as jitter.

Environment and test harness:
- Hardware: H100 (80GB) and A100-40GB nodes used. Experiments labeled H100/A100 accordingly.
- Models: Llama2-13B (fp16), a trimmed decoder-only attention stack (custom bench harness) to isolate attention kernel paths.
- Workloads: synthetic mixes to emulate production — ratio short:long = 70:30 and a bimodal 50:50. Seqs used: [16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048].
- Tools: nsys for timeline + kernel occupancy, perf / nvprof for SM occupancy + instr throughput, nvtx markers around scheduler dispatch. Custom microbench runner: bench/attention_microbench.py (see linked PR).
- Metrics captured: per-token latency (p50/p90/p95/p99), tokens/sec, kernel occupancy, L2/DRAM bandwidth, memory copy times for KV pages, kernel selection frequency.

Quick experiment matrix (subset):
- A: base (flashattention enabled, fusedops on, tile=auto, prefetch_w=2)
- B: tile=64, prefetch_w=2, fusedops on
- C: tile=128, prefetch_w=1, fusedops on
- D: tile=128, prefetch_w=3, fusedops on
- E: tile=128, prefetch_w=2, fusedops off (force paged)
- F: adaptive_tile (runtime picks tile based on seq and active_batch), prefetch_w=2, fusedops on

Notes on real runs and surprising patterns:
1) H100 base (A) with mixed 70:30 workload: p95 token latency = 15.2ms, p99 = 37.9ms, throughput 68k tokens/s. Telemetry shows kernel handoffs mid-sequence when long sequences arrive; nvtx indicates a 0.6–1.2ms delay between dispatch and kernel start for some fused kernels.

2) Changing to tile=64 (B) shrunk p95 slightly (14.1ms) but increased p99 (42.3ms). Interpretation: smaller tiles reduce per-kernel work (avoids long blocking), but increases kernel-launch overheads and scheduling pressure for fusedops.

3) tile=128 + prefetch_w=1 (C) gave best p99 stability for long sequences but lowered average TFLOPS (~4% drop) on A100 due to less overlap of prefetch and compute. p95 improved to 13.6ms and p99 dropped to 28.4ms on H100.

4) Increasing prefetch_w to 3 (D) bumped throughput but reintroduced p99 spikes for mixed bursts — likely because larger prefetching causes more DRAM reads up-front and increases L2 eviction churn when many small requests interleave with large ones. On A100 we saw DRAM burst windows aligned with spike windows in token latency.

5) Forcing fusedops off (E) reduced kernel start jitter but increased per-token latency overall (p50 up ~8%), consistent with fused path being more efficient when it runs smoothly. The fused kernels seem fragile under bursty interleaving, but essential for peak efficiency.

6) Adaptive tile heuristic (F) where runtime selects 64 for seq<=64, 128 for 65<=seq<=512, and 256 for >512: gave the best balance in mixed workloads — p95 close to C, p99 30.1ms (slightly higher than C but more stable in 50:50 bimodal tests).

Telemetry deep-dive and kernel traces:
- NVTX traces show that in many p99 events the fused attention kernel is queued for an unusually long time (0.8–2ms) after nvtx-dispatch. This correlates with scheduler contention when many small-tile kernels occupy the launch queues.
- nsys occupancy shows SM utilization dips right before p99 spikes — indicating kernel preemption or long-running memory-copy ops (prefetch) that steal bandwidth.
- Kernel-level counters: bank-conflict counters are elevated for tile sizes that are not 128-aligned with the model head-dim (in our Llama2 build head_dim=128). This suggests stride/tiling alignment matters for bank-friendliness.

Hypotheses generated from observations:
H1: Tile sizes that are not a multiple of the attention head stride (head_dim or warp tile) cause increased bank conflicts and cache-line thrashing, especially on A100.
H2: Larger prefetch windows improve throughput for homogeneous long workloads but cause L2 churn when short requests interleave, leading to p99 spikes.
H3: Fused kernels are highly efficient but sensitive to launch-time latency; small kernel fragments (tile=64) create too many small fused launches, increasing launch/dynamic-scheduler pressure.
H4: Runtime kernel selection jitter arises because kernel-choice decisions happen late (during scheduler dispatch) and sometimes switch from fused->paged mid-request if memory pressure spikes. This fallback is expensive.

Quick experiments to validate hypotheses (planned/prioritized):
- Validate H1: run microbench with head_dim mismatch toy model (set head_dim to 96, 128, 160) and sweep tile sizes. Record bank-conflict counters.
- Validate H2: synthetic interleave where long requests prefetch but then are paused (simulate preemption). Measure L2 eviction rates.
- Validate H3: instrument fused kernel launch path to aggregate number of launches per request and queue-depth; test coalescing launches where possible.
- Validate H4: add telemetry to record kernel-choice timestamp (decision_time) vs dispatch_time to quantify late fallbacks.

Immediate tactical mitigations (dev-change ideas):
1) Tile alignment policy: prefer tile sizes that are multiples/divisors of head_dim to reduce bank conflicts. Add a small alignment table in runtime.
2) Prefetch backpressure: throttle prefetch when queue_depth>threshold or when many short requests recently arrived (sliding window).
3) Fused coalescing: aggregate adjacent small tiles into single fused launches when they belong to same request to lower launch pressure.
4) Faster fallback path: pre-compile paged-fusion kernels to reduce fallback latency.

Commands and snippets used (notes to reproduce quickly):
- Run bench: python bench/attention_microbench.py --model llama13b --device h100 --mix 70-30 --tile auto --prefetch 2 --fused yes --log perf/logs/runA
- NVTX profiling: nv-nsight-cu-profiler collect -o runA.nsys --capture-range=nvtx -- python bench/attention_microbench.py ...
- Kernel counters: sudo nsys profile --sample=none --trace=cuda --stats=true ... then use nsys cupti-exporter to extract bank_conflict counters.

Raw snippets (observed numbers, H100):
- A (base): p50 6.2ms, p95 15.2ms, p99 37.9ms, tokens/s 68k
- B (tile64): p50 6.7ms, p95 14.1ms, p99 42.3ms, tokens/s 66k
- C (tile128,pref1): p50 5.9ms, p95 13.6ms, p99 28.4ms, tokens/s 65k
- D (tile128,pref3): p50 5.8ms, p95 13.8ms, p99 35.6ms, tokens/s 71k
- E (no fused): p50 7.0ms, p95 18.9ms, p99 45.1ms, tokens/s 58k
- F (adaptive): p50 6.1ms, p95 13.9ms, p99 30.1ms, tokens/s 67k

Production traces correlation attempt:
- Pulled 20 hours of traces where customers experienced tails — bins of 5-minute windows show p99 spikes correlate with sudden influx of many small requests from a few customers (spammy bursts). Also correlated with scheduled rebalancing jobs that cause background paged memory compaction on some nodes.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much does OS-level PCIe scheduling (host CPU) vs GPU SM contention contribute? We need host-level traces and to correlate with cgroups/CPU steal.
- Are there cross-tenant effects from simultaneous memory pressure (shared slab) that cause late kernel fallbacks? Need to test in fully isolated dedicated capacity to see difference.
- Can we implement a cheap runtime predictor that says "prefer fused if expected runtime > X ms" to avoid many small fused launches?

Decisions and proposed next steps (short horizon):
- Short-term (this sprint): implement tile alignment table and a metric gated prefetch throttle (PR in linked_artifacts). Add kernel-decision telemetry timestamps to quantify H4.
- Mid-term (2–4 sprints): prototype fused-launch coalescer to reduce small-launch pressure and evaluate stability.
- Long-term: explore a tiny ML predictor (linear model) inside runtime that picks tile/prefetch/fused flags per-request using recent short-term workload features. Evaluate cost of prediction vs benefit.

Todo (action items):
- [ ] Diego: instrument kernel-choice timestamp and add to logs (deadline 2026-02-24).
- [ ] Priya: run head_dim mismatch matrix on A100 and produce bank-conflict heatmap (deadline 2026-02-28).
- [ ] Ethan: isolate test in dedicated capacity and rerun mixed workload to see cross-tenant effects (deadline 2026-03-03).
- [ ] Maya: draft RFC for tile-alignment policy and prefetch backpressure heuristic (due 2026-03-07).

Notes-to-self and loose thoughts:
- There's a sweet spot between too many small fused launches and switching to paged kernels — optimizations should bias towards keeping the fused path healthy since it wins at steady-state but avoid sending it into pathological launch patterns.
- Consider exposing an observable metric in Console: "fused_launch_rate" and "prefetch_eviction_rate" to help customers debug tail latency regressions tied to workload mix.
- Small change experiment: on a couple of test nodes, pin the scheduler to prefer fused kernels by delaying non-fused kernel launches by 100–200us and see if that stabilizes tails (risky but informative).

Appendix: links to traces and artifacts
- nsys timeline files: gs://redwood-profiling/2026-02/tiling-prefetch/runA.nsys (internal)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/874 (adaptive tile machinery)
- Jira task: INF-4819 (tiling-prefetch investigation)

End of diary entry. This is a working doc; expect updates as experiments complete.
